title: Linear Maps

:::lede
Having established the structure of vector spaces, we now study the maps between them. Linear maps were defined in Chapter 4; in this chapter we organize them into vector spaces of their own, represent them by matrices once bases are chosen, and see how the matrix changes when the bases change. We end with the determinant, the most important function of a square matrix, and with the determinant and trace of a linear operator. Throughout, $k$ is a field.
:::

Recall (Definition [4.5.12](/notes/math-55a/4-5-vector-spaces#definition-4-5-12)) that a linear map $\varphi : V \to W$ between vector spaces over $k$ is a function satisfying $\varphi(u + v) = \varphi(u) + \varphi(v)$ and $\varphi(\lambda v) = \lambda\varphi(v)$ for all $u, v \in V$ and $\lambda \in k$; it then preserves all linear combinations. Just as group homomorphisms preserve the group operation, linear maps preserve both vector space operations.

:::example{5.1.1}
- The zero map $v \mapsto 0$, the identity $\id_V$, and the scaling $v \mapsto \lambda v$ for a fixed $\lambda \in k$ are linear.
- Differentiation $D : k[x] \to k[x]$, $D\big(\sum_{i} a_i x^i\big) = \sum_{i \geq 1} (i \cdot a_i) x^{i-1}$, is linear, since it acts coefficientwise. (This is the formal derivative; no limits are involved.)
- For $r \in k$, evaluation $k[x] \to k$, $f \mapsto f(r)$, is linear.
- If $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is a basis of $V$, the coordinate isomorphism $k^n \to V$, $(a_1, \ldots, a_n) \mapsto \sum a_i v_i$, is linear.
- If $V = U \oplus W$, the ***projection*** onto $U$ along $W$, sending $v = u + w$ ($u \in U$, $w \in W$) to $u$, is linear, because the decompositions of $v + v'$ and of $\lambda v$ are $(u + u') + (w + w')$ and $\lambda u + \lambda w$.
:::

:::proposition{5.1.2} Linear maps are determined by a basis
Let $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ be a basis of $V$, and let $w_1, \ldots, w_n \in W$ be arbitrary vectors. There is exactly one linear map $\varphi : V \to W$ with $\varphi(v_i) = w_i$ for all $i$, namely $$\varphi\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i w_i.$$
:::

:::proof
Uniqueness: a linear map with $\varphi(v_i) = w_i$ satisfies $\varphi\big(\sum a_i v_i\big) = \sum a_i \varphi(v_i) = \sum a_i w_i$.

Existence: every $v \in V$ has unique coordinates $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ (Proposition [4.6.9](/notes/math-55a/4-6-span-linear-independence-and-bases#proposition-4-6-9)), so the formula defines a function $\varphi : V \to W$, and $\varphi(v_i) = w_i$. If $u = \sum a_i v_i$ and $v = \sum b_i v_i$, then $u + v = \sum (a_i + b_i) v_i$ and $\lambda u = \sum (\lambda a_i) v_i$ are the coordinate expressions of $u + v$ and $\lambda u$. Hence $\varphi(u + v) = \sum (a_i + b_i) w_i = \varphi(u) + \varphi(v)$ and $\varphi(\lambda u) = \lambda \varphi(u)$.
:::

:::note
This is the ***universal property*** of a basis: specifying a linear map out of $V$ is the same as choosing where to send the basis vectors, and the choice is completely free. The same proof works for an arbitrary basis $\mathcal{B}$, finite or not: every function $\mathcal{B} \to W$ extends uniquely to a linear map $V \to W$.
:::

:::definition{5.1.3} Space of linear maps
The set of all linear maps from $V$ to $W$ is denoted $$\Hom_k(V, W) \quad \text{or simply} \quad \Hom(V, W).$$ When $V = W$, we write $\End(V) = \Hom(V, V)$ and call its elements ***endomorphisms*** of $V$, or ***linear operators*** on $V$.
:::

:::proposition{5.1.4} $\Hom(V, W)$ is a vector space
The set $\Hom(V, W)$ is a vector space over $k$, with the operations

- **addition:** $(\varphi + \psi)(v) = \varphi(v) + \psi(v)$ for all $v \in V$;
- **scalar multiplication:** $(\lambda \varphi)(v) = \lambda \cdot \varphi(v)$ for all $v \in V$.
:::

:::proof
We must check that $\varphi + \psi$ and $\lambda \varphi$ are linear when $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are. Let $u, v \in V$ and $\mu \in k$. Then $$\begin{aligned}
(\varphi + \psi)(u + v) &= \varphi(u) + \varphi(v) + \psi(u) + \psi(v) = (\varphi + \psi)(u) + (\varphi + \psi)(v), \\
(\varphi + \psi)(\mu v) &= \mu\varphi(v) + \mu\psi(v) = \mu(\varphi + \psi)(v),
\end{aligned}$$ and similarly $$\begin{aligned}
(\lambda\varphi)(u + v) &= \lambda(\varphi(u) + \varphi(v)) = (\lambda\varphi)(u) + (\lambda\varphi)(v), \\
(\lambda\varphi)(\mu v) &= \lambda\mu\varphi(v) = \mu(\lambda\varphi)(v).
\end{aligned}$$ The vector space axioms for $\Hom(V, W)$ follow from those of $W$, because the operations are defined pointwise. The zero vector is the zero map $v \mapsto 0_W$, and the additive inverse of $\varphi$ is $v \mapsto -\varphi(v)$.
:::

:::proposition{5.1.5} Composition
Let $\varphi, \varphi' \in \Hom(U, V)$, $\psi, \psi' \in \Hom(V, W)$ and $\lambda \in k$. Then $\psi \circ \varphi$ is linear, and $$\begin{gathered}
\psi \circ (\varphi + \varphi') = \psi \circ \varphi + \psi \circ \varphi', \qquad (\psi + \psi') \circ \varphi = \psi \circ \varphi + \psi' \circ \varphi, \\
(\lambda\psi) \circ \varphi = \lambda(\psi \circ \varphi) = \psi \circ (\lambda\varphi).
\end{gathered}$$ Consequently $\End(V)$ is a ring, with addition as above, multiplication given by composition, and identity element $\id_V$.
:::

:::proof
Composites of linear maps are linear by Proposition [4.5.13](/notes/math-55a/4-5-vector-spaces#proposition-4-5-13). For $u \in U$, linearity of $\psi$ gives $\psi(\varphi(u) + \varphi'(u)) = \psi(\varphi(u)) + \psi(\varphi'(u))$, which is the first identity; the second holds by the definition of $\psi + \psi'$; and the third follows from $\lambda\psi(\varphi(u)) = \psi(\lambda\varphi(u))$. For $\End(V)$: it is an abelian group under addition, composition of maps is associative with identity $\id_V$, and the first two identities are the distributive laws.
:::

The ring $\End(V)$ is not commutative when $\dim V \geq 2$ (Example [5.2.11](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#example-5-2-11)). Its units are the invertible linear operators on $V$, which form the group $\GL(V)$. We will see in Corollary [5.2.8](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#corollary-5-2-8) that $\dim \Hom(V, W) = (\dim V)(\dim W)$ when both spaces are finite-dimensional.

## <span class="num">5.1.1</span> Dependence on the Scalar Field

The notions of basis, dimension and linearity depend on the choice of the field of scalars. The same set can be a vector space over different fields, with different dimensions.

:::example{5.1.6}
**$\CC$ as a vector space over different fields:**

- Over $\CC$: $\dim_{\CC} \CC = 1$, with basis $\{1\}$. Every complex number $z$ is $z \cdot 1$.
- Over $\RR$: $\dim_{\RR} \CC = 2$, with basis $\{1, i\}$. Every complex number $a + bi$ is the $\RR$-linear combination $a \cdot 1 + b \cdot i$, and the expression is unique.
:::

More generally, if $k'$ is a subfield of $k$ (for example $\RR \subseteq \CC$ or $\QQ \subseteq \RR$), then any $k$-vector space $V$ is also a $k'$-vector space by ***restriction of scalars***: we only use scalar multiplication by elements of $k'$. In particular $k$ itself is a $k'$-vector space. A $k$-linearly independent subset of $V$ is also $k'$-linearly independent, since a $k'$-linear relation is in particular a $k$-linear relation; so $\dim_{k'} V \geq \dim_k V$.

:::proposition{5.1.7} Linearity over subfields
Let $V$ and $W$ be $k$-vector spaces and $k' \subseteq k$ a subfield. Then:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $V$ and $W$ are $k'$-vector spaces by restriction of scalars;
2. every $k$-linear map $\varphi : V \to W$ is also $k'$-linear.

Thus $\Hom_k(V, W) \subseteq \Hom_{k'}(V, W)$.
:::

:::proof
The axioms for scalar multiplication by elements of $k'$ are special cases of those for $k$, and $\varphi(\lambda v) = \lambda\varphi(v)$ for all $\lambda \in k$ holds in particular for $\lambda \in k'$.
:::

The inclusion $\Hom_k(V, W) \subseteq \Hom_{k'}(V, W)$ can be strict:

:::example{5.1.8}
**Complex conjugation is $\RR$-linear but not $\CC$-linear.** Consider $$\CC \to \CC, \quad z = a + bi \mapsto \bar{z} = a - bi.$$ It is $\RR$-linear: for $z_1, z_2 \in \CC$ and $r \in \RR$ we have $\overline{z_1 + z_2} = \bar{z}_1 + \bar{z}_2$ and $\overline{r z} = r \bar{z}$, since $\bar{r} = r$. It is not $\CC$-linear: for $\lambda = i$ and $z = 1$, $$\overline{i \cdot 1} = -i, \quad \text{but} \quad i \cdot \bar{1} = i.$$
:::

So the natural maps between spaces depend on which scalars we allow. Complex conjugation is an $\RR$-linear automorphism of $\CC$ that is not $\CC$-linear, because it does not commute with multiplication by $i$.
